[Last time](../webgpu-ripple-tank/) the waves had the tank to themselves. This time there
is a wall in the way with a hole in it.

A plane wave, a straight line of crests, comes in from the white paddle on the left and
meets the wall. The wall has one slit in it or two. What comes out of the other side?
It is the first thing most people see of how waves behave and the answer is not what
you would get by throwing something through the hole.

Red is a crest, blue is a trough and dark is flat. The faint line near the right-hand edge
is the far wall where the waves are measured for the chart below.

Try these:

- _One slit, as wide as you can make it._ **Slit width** at 32 and most of the wave goes
  straight through as a beam with a little spreading at the edges.
- _Now narrow it._ As the slit shrinks towards the **Wavelength** the beam gives way to a
  ring, as if the slit were a stone. A hole about as small as the wave does not let
  it through as a beam. It makes a new wave.
- _Two slits._ Each makes its own ring and where the rings cross they add. Crest on crest
  is a bigger crest and crest on trough is flat water so bands fan out from the wall,
  bright and dark in turn.
- _Move the slits apart with Slit spacing_ and the bands crowd closer together. Make the
  wavelength longer and they spread out.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| column: screen-inset
//| code-fold: true
//| code-summary: "Show code"
{
  // Shared WebGPU boilerplate: setup, buffers and the animation loop (lib/gpu.js)
  const gpu = await import(new URL("../lib/gpu.js", document.baseURI).href);
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  // The wave-tank kernels and bookkeeping shared by the wave posts (lib/wave.js)
  const wave = await import(new URL("../lib/wave.js", document.baseURI).href);

  // Controls are read live from their elements, so moving them does not restart
  // this cell.
  const countInput = viewof slitCount;
  const wavelengthInput = viewof wavelength;
  const widthInput = viewof slitWidth;
  const spacingInput = viewof slitSpacing;

  const { canvas, device, context, format } = await gpu.setup({
    width: 640,
    height: 360,
    resolution: "auto",
  });

  // The tank, in cells, and where things sit in it
  const W = 640;
  const H = 360;
  const cells = W * H;
  const beachWidth = 24; // cells of damping at each edge
  const sourceX = 28; // the paddle, just inside the beach
  const wallX = 196; // left side of the wall
  const wallWidth = 8;
  const screenX = 592; // the far wall, where the pattern is measured
  const amplitude = 0.25; // height of the plane wave
  const C = 0.5; // the Courant number: cells a ripple travels in one step
  const speed = 150; // wave speed, in cells a second

  // Whether each cell is water (1) or a wall (0): a wall with one slit or two,
  // centred on the middle of the tank
  function buildWall() {
    const water = new Float32Array(cells).fill(1);
    const width = widthInput.value;
    const mid = H / 2;
    // Slit centres: one in the middle, or two spacing apart
    const centres =
      countInput.value === 1
        ? [mid]
        : [mid - Math.max(spacingInput.value, width + 8) / 2, mid + Math.max(spacingInput.value, width + 8) / 2];
    for (let y = 0; y < H; y++) {
      if (centres.some((c) => Math.abs(y + 0.5 - c) < width / 2)) continue;
      for (let x = wallX; x < wallX + wallWidth; x++) water[y * W + x] = 0;
    }
    return water;
  }

  // --------------------------------------------------------------- the shaders
  // The shared kernels, with walls and the paddle switched on (lib/wave.js)
  const stepCode = wave.stepWGSL({ walls: true, source: true });
  const stepPipeline = wave.computePipeline(device, stepCode, "step");
  const tickPipeline = wave.computePipeline(device, stepCode, "tick");
  const showPipeline = wave.showPipeline(
    device,
    wave.showWGSL({ walls: true, source: true, screen: true }),
    format,
    gpu.squareLayout,
  );

  // --------------------------------------------------------------------- buffers
  // Three height arrays that take turns: one step ago, now, and the one being made
  const heights = wave.heightBuffers(gpu, device, cells);
  const waterBuffer = gpu.storageBuffer(device, buildWall());
  const clock = gpu.storageBuffer(device, new Uint32Array(1));
  // The heights now and one step ago, side by side, for reading back
  const snapshot = gpu.storageBuffer(device, new Float32Array(2 * cells));
  const params = wave.paramBlock(device);

  // Bind groups for each way the three arrays can be taking turns
  const fixed = [
    { binding: 0, resource: { buffer: params.buffer } },
    { binding: 1, resource: { buffer: waterBuffer } },
  ];
  const clockEntry = { binding: 5, resource: { buffer: clock } };
  const stepGroups = wave.turnGroups(device, stepPipeline, heights, [...fixed, clockEntry], wave.stepSlots);
  const tickGroup = device.createBindGroup({
    layout: tickPipeline.getBindGroupLayout(0),
    entries: [clockEntry],
  });
  const showGroups = wave.turnGroups(device, showPipeline, heights, fixed, wave.showSlots);
  const cornerBuffer = gpu.unitSquare(device);

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------- the state
  let turn = 0; // which of the three arrays is "one step ago"
  let stepCount = 0;
  let sourceStart = 0;

  // What the chart is built from: how big the wave is down the far wall, averaged
  const readback = gpu.readback(device, [{ buffer: snapshot, bytes: 2 * cells * 4 }]);
  const sampleEvery = 5; // frames between readbacks
  let frameCount = 0;
  let epoch = 0; // bumped when the tank is cleared, so a read in flight is dropped
  let statsStart = 0; // step at which the averaged pattern last restarted
  const brightness = new Float64Array(H);
  let averaged = 0;

  const [screenHost] = charts.children;
  const draw = ui.plotter(Plot);

  // The classic prediction for the pattern on a distant wall, for waves of this
  // wavelength through slits of width a that are d apart (d = 0 for one slit)
  function prediction() {
    const lambda = wavelengthInput.value;
    const a = widthInput.value;
    const d = countInput.value === 1 ? 0 : Math.max(spacingInput.value, a + 8);
    const distance = screenX - (wallX + wallWidth / 2);
    const rows = [];
    for (let y = -H / 2 + 20; y <= H / 2 - 20; y += 2) {
      const s = y / Math.hypot(y, distance);
      const alpha = (Math.PI * a * s) / lambda;
      const beta = (Math.PI * d * s) / lambda;
      const envelope = alpha === 0 ? 1 : (Math.sin(alpha) / alpha) ** 2;
      rows.push({ y, I: envelope * (d === 0 ? 1 : Math.cos(beta) ** 2) });
    }
    return rows;
  }

  function drawChart() {
    const measured = [];
    if (averaged > 0) {
      let top = 0;
      for (let y = 20; y < H - 20; y++) top = Math.max(top, brightness[y]);
      for (let y = 20; y < H - 20; y++) measured.push({ y: y - H / 2, I: brightness[y] / top });
    }
    draw(screenHost, {
      height: 220,
      x: { label: "position along the far wall (cells from the middle)", grid: true },
      y: { label: "wave brightness (relative)", grid: true, domain: [0, 1.05] },
      marks: [
        Plot.line(measured, { x: "y", y: "I", stroke: "#FF4834" }),
        Plot.line(prediction(), {
          x: "y",
          y: "I",
          stroke: "currentColor",
          strokeOpacity: 0.7,
          strokeDasharray: "4 3",
        }),
      ],
    });
  }

  // Wait for the start-up transient to leave the far wall before averaging
  function settled() {
    const travel = (screenX - sourceX + 6 * wavelengthInput.value) / C;
    return stepCount - statsStart > travel;
  }

  function onData(buffer) {
    if (settled()) {
      // Two heights a step apart fix the size of a wave of one frequency, whatever
      // moment they are taken at: A^2 = (s^2 + p^2 - 2 s p cos w) / sin^2 w, for the
      // height s now and p one step ago, with w the radians a step
      const now = new Float32Array(buffer, 0, cells);
      const before = new Float32Array(buffer, cells * 4, cells);
      const w = (2 * Math.PI * C) / wavelengthInput.value;
      const cos = Math.cos(w);
      const sin2 = Math.sin(w) ** 2;
      for (let y = 0; y < H; y++) {
        const s = now[y * W + screenX];
        const p = before[y * W + screenX];
        brightness[y] += (s * s + p * p - 2 * s * p * cos) / sin2;
      }
      averaged++;
    }
    drawChart();
  }

  // Empty the tank and start the paddle again
  function restart() {
    epoch++;
    device.queue.writeBuffer(waterBuffer, 0, buildWall());
    const zeros = new Float32Array(cells);
    for (const buffer of heights) device.queue.writeBuffer(buffer, 0, zeros);
    sourceStart = stepCount;
    statsStart = stepCount;
    brightness.fill(0);
    averaged = 0;
    drawChart();
  }

  const on = (element, handler) => {
    element.addEventListener("input", handler);
    invalidation.then(() => element.removeEventListener("input", handler));
  };
  for (const input of [countInput, wavelengthInput, widthInput, spacingInput]) on(input, restart);

  const restartButton = ui.button({ label: "Restart", onClick: restart });
  drawChart();

  let owed = 0; // steps due but not yet done
  let lastTime = null;
  const groups = wave.groups(W, H);

  function frame(ms) {
    const dt = lastTime === null ? 0 : Math.min((ms - lastTime) / 1000, 0.1);
    lastTime = ms;
    const lambda = wavelengthInput.value;

    owed += (speed / C) * dt;
    const count = Math.min(Math.floor(owed), 40);
    owed = Math.min(owed - count, 1);

    params.write({
      width: W,
      height: H,
      ...wave.beach({ C, width: beachWidth }),
      screenX,
      sourceX,
      sourceStart,
      ...wave.paddle({ C, wavelength: lambda, amplitude }),
      gain: wave.heightGain,
    });

    const encoder = device.createCommandEncoder();
    const compute = encoder.beginComputePass();
    for (let s = 0; s < count; s++) {
      compute.setPipeline(stepPipeline);
      compute.setBindGroup(0, stepGroups[turn]);
      compute.dispatchWorkgroups(groups.x, groups.y);
      compute.setPipeline(tickPipeline);
      compute.setBindGroup(0, tickGroup);
      compute.dispatchWorkgroups(1);
      turn = (turn + 1) % 3;
    }
    compute.end();
    stepCount += count;

    const sample = !readback.pending && ++frameCount % sampleEvery === 0;
    if (sample) {
      encoder.copyBufferToBuffer(heights[(turn + 1) % 3], 0, snapshot, 0, cells * 4);
      encoder.copyBufferToBuffer(heights[turn], 0, snapshot, cells * 4, cells * 4);
      readback.copy(encoder);
    }

    const pass = gpu.beginRenderPass(encoder, context);
    pass.setPipeline(showPipeline);
    pass.setBindGroup(0, showGroups[turn]);
    pass.setVertexBuffer(0, cornerBuffer);
    pass.draw(6);
    pass.end();
    device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]);

    if (sample) {
      const mine = epoch;
      readback.read((buffer) => {
        if (mine === epoch) onData(buffer);
      });
    }
  }

  gpu.run(invalidation, device, frame);

  // The canvas with the controls laid over its corner
  yield ui.stage(canvas, [countInput, wavelengthInput, widthInput, spacingInput, restartButton]);
}
```

## Analysis

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
charts = {
  // An empty host; the simulation cell above draws into it as data arrives
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  return ui.chartHosts(["screen"]);
}
```

How bright the waves are along the far wall, the faint line on the right of the tank. The
solid line is what the tank gives, averaged over many moments and the dashed line is the
classic prediction for waves through slits of width $a$ that are $d$ apart, a long way
from the wall. It has two parts. One slit gives only the broad hump. It gets wider as the
slit gets narrower. Two slits add fine fringes inside it, bright where the paths from the two slits
differ by a whole number of wavelengths ($d \sin\theta = m\lambda$) and dark halfway
between. Change the **Wavelength**, **Slit width** or **Slit spacing** and both lines move
in the way the formula says. They do not agree exactly because the far wall is not very far
away and the tank is two-dimensional.

## A letter from Leiden

Christiaan Huygens said in a treatise published in 1690 that every point on a wave can be
treated as a new source of little circular waves and that the wave a moment later is what
they add up to. A gap in a wall is then easy to understand: the wave arrives, the points
in the gap each start a ring and nothing is left to cancel the rings except one another.
Two gaps are two sets of rings.

Around 1800, Thomas Young used the same picture to argue that light is a wave. In his
lectures he showed what two sets of water waves do in a shallow tank with a lamp
underneath and then showed that light passed through two slits makes bright and dark
bands of the same kind. That is the two slits in the tank above and it is still the
standard way to show waves in a classroom.

## How the computer does it

The tank is the one from last time with one change. Each cell has a number (1 for water
and 0 for wall) and the rule uses it when a cell looks at its neighbours. A wall is a cell
with nothing to pull on. There is no special case for a slit: a slit is just a gap in the
zeros so the width and spacing sliders cost nothing extra and the tank is
rebuilt in a moment when they move.

The chart is measured in the tank. A few times a second the GPU hands back the heights of
every cell. The size of a wave is how high it gets over a whole cycle and a single snapshot
catches it part-way through. But two snapshots a step apart are enough to work it out
because a wave of one frequency changes in a known way from one step to the next. The page
does that along the far wall and squares it to get a brightness then averages over many
readings. It only starts counting once the first crests have had time to reach the far wall.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The pattern, in formulas

For waves of wavelength $\lambda$ through slits of width $a$ with centres $d$ apart, seen
at an angle $\theta$ a long way from the wall, the brightness is

$$I(\theta) \propto \cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi d \sin\theta}{\lambda}\right) \left(\frac{\sin \alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\pi a \sin\theta}{\lambda}.$$

The cosine is the fringes from the two slits, with bright bands where
$d \sin\theta = m\lambda$. The second factor is the hump from the width of one slit and its
first dark place is where $a \sin\theta = \lambda$. With one slit there is only the hump
($d = 0$ takes the cosine to 1). On a wall a distance $L$ away the fringes are about
$\lambda L / d$ apart.
:::

## Sources

- Huygens, C. (1690), _Traité de la lumière_ (Leiden).
- Young, T., lectures to the Royal Society, around 1800, as described in
  [Young's interference experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_interference_experiment).
